### 71. Inheritance vs Composition · Medium

*java · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## java-inheritance-vs-composition` then `match: A developer wants to reuse code for a reporting system. They write the following Java class. Which line introduces a des`</sub>

**Question**

A developer wants to reuse code for a reporting system. They write the following Java class. Which line introduces a design flaw that violates the principle 'favor composition over inheritance'?

**Options**

A. class Report {
B.     void generate() { System.out.println("Generating report"); }
C. }
D. class PdfReport extends Report {
E.     @Override void generate() { System.out.println("Generating PDF"); }
F. }
G. class CsvReport extends Report {
H.     @Override void generate() { System.out.println("Generating CSV"); }
I. }
J. class HtmlReport extends Report {
K.     @Override void generate() { System.out.println("Generating HTML"); }
L. }

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: D. class PdfReport extends Report {

**Reference answer**

Line 4 (`class PdfReport extends Report`) is the flaw: it uses class inheritance to reuse the `generate` method, coupling each report type to the `Report` superclass. Adding a new report format requires a new subclass, and changes to `Report` can break all subclasses. Composition with a `ReportRenderer` interface would allow swapping rendering behavior without subclassing.

**Graded on**

- Class inheritance creates a tight is-a coupling between `PdfReport` and `Report`.
- Adding a new format requires a new subclass, which is brittle.
- Composition would delegate to a `ReportRenderer` component, allowing runtime flexibility.
- The principle 'favor composition over inheritance' applies when behavior varies independently of the class hierarchy.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Inheritance in Java takes two forms. Class inheritance via `extends` lets one subclass inherit fields, methods, and implementation from exactly one superclass, creating an is-a relationship. Interface inheritance via `implements` makes a class a subtype of the interface and lets it inherit abstract and default method contracts; a class can implement many interfaces. Composition, by contrast, is a has-a relationship: an object holds another object as a field and delegates behavior to it, without inheriting its implementation.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers ask this to test whether you understand the design tradeoff between code reuse and coupling. They want to see that you can choose the right mechanism for a given design, not just recite definitions. A strong answer distinguishes class inheritance, interface inheritance, and composition, and explains why composition is often preferred.

## The core idea

The real difference is coupling and substitutability. Class inheritance gives a subclass the superclass's API and implementation, so the subclass is tightly bound to the superclass at compile time and cannot swap behavior at runtime. Composition keeps the component behind the owning object's API and uses explicit delegation, so components can be replaced, mocked, or changed without altering the owner. Java's single class inheritance makes deep hierarchies brittle, while interfaces provide multiple subtyping without implementation coupling. Use inheritance when a class truly is a substitutable subtype; otherwise, compose objects and delegate.

## Key points

- Java class inheritance uses `extends` and gives a subclass one superclass; Java interface inheritance uses `implements` and allows many supertypes, including inherited default methods.
- Inheritance models an is-a relationship and should satisfy the Liskov Substitution Principle; composition models a has-a relationship and delegates to an owned component.
- Composition reduces compile-time coupling and allows behavior to be changed at runtime by replacing the component, whereas inheritance fixes behavior in the class hierarchy.
- Composition is stronger than aggregation: in composition the whole owns the part and the part's lifetime is tied to the whole; in aggregation the part can exist independently.
- The design principle 'favor composition over inheritance' means use interfaces and delegation for code reuse by default, and reserve class inheritance for true subtype relationships.

## Your 60-second answer

Java gives us two ways to reuse code: inheritance and composition. Inheritance with `extends` is an is-a relationship: a subclass inherits the superclass's fields and methods and can override them. A class can extend only one class, though it can implement many interfaces, which is interface inheritance rather than class inheritance. Composition is a has-a relationship: an object holds a reference to another object and delegates work to it. The tradeoff is coupling: inheritance gives reuse for free but binds the subclass to the superclass implementation, so changes in the parent can break subclasses. Composition requires writing forwarding methods, but you can swap the component at runtime and keep classes decoupled. In general, prefer composition for reuse, and reserve class inheritance for true is-a substitutability.

## If they dig deeper

**What does it mean to favor composition over inheritance?**

It is a design principle from the Gang of Four: use object composition and delegation as the default for code reuse, and use class inheritance only when you need subtype polymorphism and a genuine is-a relationship. Composition gives looser coupling and runtime flexibility.

**When would you still choose inheritance over composition?**

When you have a stable base class and subclasses that are truly substitutable for it, satisfying the Liskov Substitution Principle. Framework template methods and cases where you need to override protected methods to plug into an existing algorithm are also common legitimate uses.

**What is the difference between aggregation and composition?**

Both are has-a relationships, but aggregation has an independent lifecycle: the part can exist without the whole and may be shared. Composition is stronger: the whole owns the part, its lifetime is tied to the whole, and the part usually cannot exist independently, such as a Car owning its Engine.

**How do Java interfaces affect the inheritance-vs-composition tradeoff?**

Interfaces provide subtyping without implementation inheritance: a class can implement many interfaces, so you get polymorphic behavior without being locked into one superclass. Since Java 8, default methods allow some code reuse through interfaces, but interfaces still cannot hold state; for reuse that needs state, composition is usually preferred.

**What is the fragile base class problem, and how does composition avoid it?**

Changes to a superclass can silently change or break subclasses because subclasses depend on inherited implementation details, especially when they override methods or rely on self-calls. Composition hides the component behind the owning class's API and delegates explicitly, so internal changes to the component do not leak into the owner's contract or subclasses.

## Worked example

A common example is a reporting system. With inheritance, `Report` might have `generate()` and subclasses `PdfReport` and `CsvReport` override it. Adding HTML means a new subclass and may duplicate code. Instead, use composition: `interface ReportRenderer { String render(Data data); }`, `PdfRenderer` and `CsvRenderer` implement it, and `Report` holds a `ReportRenderer`. `Report.generate()` calls `renderer.render(data)`. A caller can construct `new Report(new PdfRenderer())` or `new Report(new CsvRenderer())`; the behavior changes without creating new `Report` subclasses. If you later add `HtmlRenderer`, only a new component is needed. Composition keeps the rendering algorithm behind a small interface and lets the `Report` class change behavior at runtime, whereas inheritance would freeze the behavior into the class hierarchy.

## Common traps

- Calling interface implementation 'not inheritance' — Java treats implementing an interface as interface inheritance/subtyping, distinct from class implementation inheritance.
- Using `extends` just to grab utility methods from a concrete class, such as extending `ArrayList` when the class is not truly a list subtype; this exposes inherited implementation and breaks encapsulation.
- Claiming composition is always better and never using inheritance; inheritance is appropriate for stable is-a hierarchies and framework extension points.
- Forgetting that composition requires explicit delegation; unlike inheritance, fields and methods of the composed object are not automatically available on the containing class.

</details>

### 72. Greedy · Medium

*dsa · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## greedy` then `match: The following code attempts to solve the Gas Station problem`</sub>

**Question**

The following code attempts to solve the Gas Station problem: given gas and cost arrays, return the starting station index if a circuit is possible, else -1. Which line contains the bug?

```
1  def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
2      total_tank = 0
3      curr_tank = 0
4      start = 0
5      for i in range(len(gas)):
6          total_tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
7          curr_tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
8          if curr_tank < 0:
9              start = i + 1
10             curr_tank = 0
11     return start if total_tank >= 0 else -1
```

**Options**

A. 1  def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
B. 2      total_tank = 0
C. 3      curr_tank = 0
D. 4      start = 0
E. 5      for i in range(len(gas)):
F. 6          total_tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
G. 7          curr_tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
H. 8          if curr_tank < 0:
I. 9              start = i + 1
J. 10             curr_tank = 0
K. 11     return start if total_tank >= 0 else -1

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: I. 9              start = i + 1

**Reference answer**

Line 9 is the bug: it sets start to i + 1 unconditionally when curr_tank becomes negative, but the correct greedy reset should set start to i + 1 only if the total tank from the previous start to i is negative. In the standard algorithm, the reset is correct because the total tank from the previous start to i is exactly curr_tank, which is negative, so i + 1 is indeed the next candidate. However, the bug is that the code does not check whether the total tank is negative before resetting; it resets based on curr_tank alone, which can be negative even when the total tank is nonnegative, leading to an incorrect start index. The correct condition is to reset only when total_tank < 0, not curr_tank < 0.

**Graded on**

- The reset condition should be based on total_tank, not curr_tank.
- curr_tank can be negative while total_tank is nonnegative, causing an incorrect reset.
- The correct algorithm resets start to i + 1 only when the cumulative sum from the current start becomes negative.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

A greedy algorithm builds a solution by choosing the best immediate option at each step, then fixing that choice and reducing the problem. It never revisits earlier decisions, so it often runs in O(n) or O(n log n) time. Greedy is correct when the problem has optimal substructure and the greedy choice property: some locally optimal choice is part of an optimal solution.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use greedy problems to test whether a candidate can identify when short-sighted local choices are actually safe, and whether they can articulate a correctness argument rather than just code an intuition. The listed problems, including Maximum Subarray, Jump Game, Gas Station, Valid Parenthesis String, Jump Game II, and Partition Labels, appear frequently at companies such as Flipkart, PhonePe, Adobe, TikTok, LinkedIn, and Nielsen.

## The core idea

The central skill is not picking the greedy rule, but proving that no future consequence can make a locally better choice globally worse. A greedy algorithm commits to each decision, so a wrong rule silently produces the wrong answer. The standard proof technique is an exchange argument: take an optimal solution and swap its first differing decision for the greedy decision without making it worse. For prefix-sum-like problems such as Maximum Subarray, the rule of discarding a negative prefix is safe because any subarray extending a negative prefix can be improved by starting after it. Always state the invariant the greedy choice maintains before writing code.

## Key points

- A greedy algorithm picks the locally best option at each step and then commits to it, never backtracking, which commonly leads to O(n) or O(n log n) solutions.
- Greedy correctness requires both optimal substructure and the greedy choice property; without them, a local choice can block a better global solution.
- An exchange argument proves correctness by transforming any optimal solution into one that includes the greedy choice without worsening cost.
- Kadane's algorithm for Maximum Subarray can be viewed as greedy: it keeps the best suffix sum ending at the current index and starts fresh when the previous suffix sum is negative.
- In Jump Game II, maintaining the current jump's reach and the farthest index reachable from it yields the minimum jump count in O(n).

## Your 60-second answer

A greedy algorithm builds an answer by taking the best local decision at each step and never revising it. It works when the problem has the greedy choice property: a locally optimal choice can be part of an optimal solution. For example, in Jump Game we keep the farthest reachable index and update it at each position; if it covers the last index, the answer is true. In Gas Station we scan net fuel and reset the candidate whenever the running tank becomes negative. The tradeoff is that greedy is fast, usually O(n), but if the problem lacks that property, a short-sighted choice can destroy optimality and you need dynamic programming. The practical skill is being able to prove the greedy rule is safe before coding.

## If they dig deeper

**How do you prove that a greedy algorithm is correct?**

Usually with an exchange argument: take any optimal solution and show you can replace its first choice that differs from the greedy choice with the greedy choice without making the solution worse, then repeat. You also need to show that the subproblem remaining after the greedy choice still contains an optimal solution.

**Why does greedy work for fractional knapsack but not for the 0/1 knapsack?**

In fractional knapsack, taking as much of the highest value-per-weight item as possible is safe because the remaining capacity can be filled with a fraction of the next best item. In 0/1 knapsack, a single high-density item can consume capacity that a combination of lower-density items needs to achieve a higher total value, so no single-item choice is guaranteed to lead to an optimal solution.

**Why is it safe to reset the starting candidate to i + 1 when the tank becomes negative in Gas Station?**

At the point the tank goes negative, the current candidate from start to i has a negative net fuel. Any station j between start and i would have a nonnegative prefix from start to j-1 before the reset, but the segment from j to i would still be negative, since the total from start to i is negative and start-to-j-1 is nonnegative, so j cannot reach i. Therefore all starts through i are eliminated, and if total gas is at least total cost the first index after the last deficit must work.

**Can you explain the greedy solution for Valid Parenthesis String using low and high counts?**

Maintain two counters: low is the minimum possible number of open parentheses and high is the maximum possible number after processing the current character. On '(' both increase; on ')' both decrease; on '*' increase high and decrease low. If high becomes negative, there are more closing parentheses than possible opens, so invalid. Low is reset to 0 because negative open count is not possible. At the end the string is valid iff low equals 0.

## Worked example

Take gas=[1,2,3,4,5] and cost=[3,4,5,1,2]. The per-station net fuel is [-2,-2,-2,3,3], and total net fuel is 0, so a circuit is possible. Starting the scan at index 0, the tank goes -2, reset to index 1; then -2 again, reset to 2; then -2 again, reset to 3. Starting at index 3, the tank after reaching station 4 is 3, after station 0 is 6, after station 1 is 4, after station 2 is 2, and after completing the lap is 0. The algorithm returns 3, the unique valid start.

## Common traps

- Assuming a greedy rule is correct because it feels right, without testing it on small counterexamples or proving the exchange argument.
- Using greedy for 0/1 knapsack or coin change with arbitrary denominations when the choice can consume capacity that a combination of smaller items needs.
- In Gas Station, returning the station after a reset without first checking that total gas is at least total cost, which gives an index even when no circuit exists.
- In Maximum Subarray, resetting the running sum to zero and returning zero for an all-negative array when the correct maximum must be a single element.

</details>

### 73. Load balancing · Medium

*system_design · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## sd-load-balancing` then `match: A load balancer distributes traffic across three backend ser`</sub>

**Question**

A load balancer distributes traffic across three backend servers using the following configuration. Which line is the bottleneck that will cause uneven load distribution under a workload of long-lived, variable-duration connections?

**Options**

A. algorithm: round_robin
B. health_check: enabled
C. servers: [A, B, C]
D. layer: L4

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: A. algorithm: round_robin

**Reference answer**

Line 3 is the bottleneck. Round robin cycles through servers without considering active connection counts, so with long-lived connections of varying duration, it can pile many connections onto one server while others sit idle. Least connections would adapt to the current load.

**Graded on**

- Round robin assumes uniform request duration and server capacity.
- Long-lived, variable-duration connections make round robin distribute unevenly.
- Least connections selects the server with the fewest active connections.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Load balancing distributes incoming network or application traffic across multiple backend servers using a configurable algorithm and health checks. It prevents a single server from becoming a bottleneck, improves throughput and response time, and enables horizontal scaling by adding or removing servers without changing clients. Load balancers can operate at Layer 4 (transport, TCP/UDP) or Layer 7 (application, HTTP).

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use load balancing to test whether you can design for scale, availability, and failure handling. They expect you to choose an algorithm for the workload, explain where balancing happens in a multi-tier architecture, and describe how health checks and failover keep the system online.

## The core idea

A load balancer sits in front of a pool of servers and chooses which server receives each request based on an algorithm. It stops serving unhealthy instances and lets you add or remove capacity without disrupting clients. The algorithm matters less than correct health checking and the distinction between Layer 4 (connection-level) and Layer 7 (request/content-level) routing. For stateful workloads you may need session affinity; for uneven server capacity, weighted algorithms.

## Key points

- A health check marks backend instances as healthy or unhealthy; the load balancer routes only to healthy instances and can trigger failover.
- Round robin cycles sequentially and suits uniform, stateless servers; weighted round robin adds capacity weights.
- Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest active connections and adapts to uneven workloads.
- Layer 4 load balancers route using IP and TCP/UDP data, while Layer 7 load balancers inspect HTTP headers, cookies, or paths.
- High availability requires the load balancer itself to be redundant, often via active-passive pairs or multiple load balancers with DNS failover.

## Your 60-second answer

A load balancer sits in front of backend servers and distributes incoming requests across them. It avoids overloading one machine, keeps latency low, and lets the system tolerate server failures. The balancer uses periodic health checks to take unhealthy servers out of rotation, and an algorithm to select a target: round robin, least connections, or IP hash are common. Layer 4 balancers route on connection-level data, while Layer 7 balancers can inspect HTTP and route by path or cookie. The main trade-off is that the load balancer adds an extra hop and can become a single point of failure, so production systems deploy it in pairs or rely on managed cloud balancers.

## If they dig deeper

**What is the difference between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing?**

Layer 4 balances using transport-layer data like IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports, without inspecting payload, so it is fast and works for any TCP/UDP protocol. Layer 7 terminates and inspects HTTP, enabling routing by URL path, headers, or cookies, and can also handle TLS termination, but uses more CPU.

**How do health checks work, and what happens when an instance fails?**

Active health checks periodically send TCP, HTTP, or gRPC probes to each backend; passive checks infer health from actual request outcomes. After a configured number of failures, the load balancer marks the instance unhealthy and removes it from rotation, so new requests go to healthy servers; it re-adds the instance once checks pass again.

**Which algorithm would you choose for a service with long-lived connections of varying duration?**

Least connections or least response time is better because round robin can accidentally pile many long-lived connections onto one server. A Layer 4 least-connections balancer works well for raw TCP; if content-based routing is needed, use a Layer 7 balancer with HTTP metrics.

**How do you maintain session state when users need to stay on the same server?**

You can use session affinity, or sticky sessions, via a cookie or IP hash so a user returns to the same backend. This hurts even distribution and failover, so the stronger approach is to keep sessions in a shared store such as Redis and let any server serve the request.

**How do you make the load balancer itself highly available?**

Deploy at least two load balancers in an active-passive or active-active pair, share a virtual IP using VRRP or a cloud service, and use health checks between the balancers so a standby takes over automatically. DNS can also point to multiple balancers, and anycast can route clients to the nearest healthy one.

## Worked example

Three servers sit behind a load balancer. With round robin and all healthy, requests 1 through 9 are assigned A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C. Now suppose each request holds its connection for a different length of time: A is handling 5 active requests, B 2, and C 0. A least-connections balancer sends the next request to C because it has the fewest current connections, even though round robin might have pointed to A. If C then fails, health checks mark it unhealthy after repeated failed probes and remove it from the pool, so traffic is distributed only across A and B until C passes checks again.

## Common traps

- Choosing an algorithm only for fairness without accounting for variable request duration or heterogeneous server capacity.
- Forgetting that the load balancer itself is a single point of failure unless deployed redundantly.
- Using IP-hash or sticky sessions as a substitute for shared session storage, which breaks failover and horizontal scaling.
- Ignoring health checks: a balancer that routes to a dead instance will still send user traffic and cause errors.

</details>

### 75. Greedy · Medium

*dsa · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## greedy` then `match: Consider the following greedy algorithm for the Gas Station `</sub>

**Question**

Consider the following greedy algorithm for the Gas Station problem, where gas and cost are arrays of length n. The algorithm scans stations and resets the starting candidate when the tank becomes negative. Which line contains the bug that can cause an incorrect result?

```
1  def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
2      total = 0
3      tank = 0
4      start = 0
5      for i in range(len(gas)):
6          total += gas[i] - cost[i]
7          tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
8          if tank < 0:
9              start = i + 1
10             tank = 0
11     return start if total >= 0 else -1
```

**Options**

A. 1  def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
B. 2      total = 0
C. 3      tank = 0
D. 4      start = 0
E. 5      for i in range(len(gas)):
F. 6          total += gas[i] - cost[i]
G. 7          tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
H. 8          if tank < 0:
I. 9              start = i + 1
J. 10             tank = 0
K. 11     return start if total >= 0 else -1

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: K. 11     return start if total >= 0 else -1

**Reference answer**

Line 11 is the bug: it returns start whenever total >= 0, but start may be n if the last station caused a reset. In that case, the algorithm returns an index that is out of bounds, even though a valid circuit may exist starting at an earlier station. The correct return should be start % n when total >= 0.

**Graded on**

- The algorithm correctly resets the candidate start to i + 1 when the tank becomes negative.
- If the tank becomes negative at the last station, start becomes n, which is not a valid index.
- The condition total >= 0 only guarantees that a circuit exists, not that the current start is valid.
- The fix is to return start % n when total >= 0, or to handle the wrap-around explicitly.

### 76. Elevator System Design · Medium

*lld · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## lld-elevator-system-design` then `match: You are reviewing a single-elevator controller that uses LOO`</sub>

**Question**

You are reviewing a single-elevator controller that uses LOOK scheduling. The car is at floor 2, direction UP, with pending hall requests: UP at 8, UP at 5, DOWN at 4, and an in-car destination 7. The controller's stop list is built by the following code. Which line causes the car to serve the DOWN request at floor 4 on the UP pass, violating direction-matching?

**Options**

A. stops = []
B. for req in pending_requests:
C.     stops.append(req.floor)
D. stops.sort()
E. if direction == UP:
F.     stops = [f for f in stops if f >= current_floor]
G. else:
H.     stops = [f for f in stops if f <= current_floor]
I. return stops

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: C.     stops.append(req.floor)

**Reference answer**

Line 3 adds every pending request to the stop list without checking its direction. The DOWN request at floor 4 is added even though the car is moving UP, so the car will stop at floor 4 on the UP pass. The fix is to filter requests by direction before adding them to the stop list.

**Graded on**

- Hall requests carry a direction; in-car requests do not.
- LOOK serves only requests in the current direction before reversing.
- The bug is adding all requests regardless of direction.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Elevator system design in an LLD interview means modeling a building with one or more elevator cars, floors, and requests: hall calls (with direction) and in-car button presses (target floor only). The design centers on each car's state (moving up, moving down, stopped with doors opening/closing, idle), a dispatcher that assigns hall calls, and a scheduling policy that decides stop order. Typical policies are FCFS, SCAN, and LOOK; LOOK is usually the right default because it serves current-direction stops before reversing without traveling to extreme empty floors.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use this to test whether you can turn an everyday physical system into explicit classes, state transitions, and concurrency boundaries. They look for a clean separation among request intake, the scheduling/dispatching layer, and each elevator's controller, plus reasoning about fairness, wait time, and deadlock-free door/movement sequencing.

## The core idea

An elevator is a finite state machine with a direction and a set of pending stops; requests are just floor plus optional direction data. A central dispatcher owns assignment of hall requests if there are multiple cars, while each car owns its internal stop list. The simplest defensible scheduling policy is LOOK: keep serving the furthest request in the current direction, then reverse only when no current-direction requests remain. This prevents starvation in the common case, avoids useless travel to building extremes, and is easy to explain and test. More advanced policies add estimated time to arrival or sectoring, but they only matter when the interviewer asks to optimize multi-car assignment after the basic design is solid.

## Key points

- An elevator has at least four states: moving up, moving down, stopped with doors open, and idle; transitions are triggered by reaching a floor, door timers, or new assigned requests.
- Hall requests carry a direction (up/down), while internal car requests specify only a destination floor; both must be modeled explicitly.
- LOOK scheduling serves requests in the current direction until no further request exists in that direction, then reverses, avoiding unnecessary full-floor scans and starvation.
- With multiple elevators, a central dispatcher assigns hall requests to one car using a policy such as shortest expected time, while each car owns its internal queue.
- Thread safety matters: multiple request sources (hall buttons, internal panels, dispatcher) update shared lists, so use synchronized structures or a single-threaded event loop per controller.

## Your 60-second answer

I would model each elevator as a state machine with current floor, direction, and a queue of assigned stops. Hall requests carry a direction; in-car requests are just a target floor. I’d use a central dispatcher for multiple elevators: it owns hall request assignment and hands each hall call to exactly one car based on a cost estimate, typically travel time plus stops. For per-car scheduling, I’d implement LOOK: the car keeps moving in its current direction, serves all same-direction requests ahead of it, then reverses. This is simple, avoids starvation, and wastes no trips to empty extremes. The main trade-off is that LOOK can ignore a nearby opposite-direction hall call while assigned to another car, causing some wait; you can improve assignment with better scoring, but then you need more testing to avoid races and duplicate stops.

## If they dig deeper

**What are the core classes and responsibilities in this system?**

ElevatorSystem holds the dispatching policy and collection of elevators; ElevatorCar owns current floor, direction, door state, and its stop list; Request has target floor plus direction for hall calls; Direction and DoorState are enums; each floor has hall buttons, and the car has an internal panel.

**Why use LOOK instead of SCAN or FCFS?**

FCFS can thrash the car across the building and gives terrible average wait times. SCAN moves to the physical extremes even if no one is there, adding empty travel. LOOK stops at the farthest actual request in the current direction, so it preserves the simplicity of SCAN while removing wasted floor visits.

**How do you prevent a hall request from being assigned to two elevators at once?**

The central dispatcher is the single writer for hall request assignments. It reads pending hall calls, computes a score for each car, assigns the request exactly once, and marks it assigned. No elevator controller consumes an unassigned hall call; they only react to assignments pushed to them.

**What happens to a request that arrives while an elevator is already moving in the opposite direction?**

The dispatcher can hold it until an idle car passes or assign it to a car whose current direction matches, but usually it must not interrupt the moving car to reverse. In a single-car LOOK implementation, opposite-direction calls are queued until the car completes its current pass and reverses; if no matching request existed, the car simply turns around at the farthest stop.

**Can LOOK starve requests if new requests keep arriving in front of a moving car?**

Yes, without safeguards a stream of same-direction requests ahead of the car can keep pushing the reversal point upward, so requests behind the car wait indefinitely. Mitigations include freezing the direction at the start of a pass, assigning timestamps and prioritizing old requests, or switching to a bounded SCAN-like cycle; none of these gives a strict worst-case wait bound unless you explicitly add aging or admission control.

## Worked example

Consider one elevator for a 10-floor building: current floor 2, direction UP, pending hall requests UP at 8 and UP at 5, a hall request DOWN at 4, and an in-car destination 7. With LOOK and direction-matching, the car first serves the same-direction requests above it: floor 5, then 7, then 8. It skips floor 4 on the UP pass because that caller wants to go DOWN. Once at 8 with no more UP requests, the car reverses and serves floor 4 on the down pass. The stop order is 5 → 7 → 8 → 4. If SCAN were used instead, after 8 the car would still travel empty to floor 10 before reversing, which is the waste LOOK removes.

## Common traps

- Starting to draw class diagrams before asking whether the building has one elevator or many; this changes whether you need a dispatcher at all.
- Treating a hall request as just a floor without a direction; this makes an elevator open for a passenger heading the opposite way and degrades the whole schedule.
- Forgetting door timing or emergency stop states, then hand-waving state transitions, which leaves impossible sequences like doors opening while moving.
- Proposing an 'optimal' scheduling algorithm without a clear cost metric; in an interview this usually signals you have not defined what you are optimizing.

</details>

*lld · gate confidence 0.7*

**Options**

A. public class StockMarket {
B.     private DisplayA displayA;
C.     private DisplayB displayB;
D.     public void notifyDisplays() {
E.         displayA.update(price);
F.         displayB.update(price);
G.     }
H. }

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: D.     public void notifyDisplays() {

**Reference answer**

Line 4 is the flaw: the StockMarket class holds concrete references to DisplayA and DisplayB, coupling the subject to specific observer implementations. This violates the Observer pattern's intent of depending on an abstraction, so adding a new display requires modifying StockMarket.

**Graded on**

- The Observer pattern decouples subjects from observers by depending on an interface.
- Concrete observer references force the subject to change when new observers are added.
- A List<Observer> with an Observer interface would allow dynamic registration.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Design patterns are named, reusable solution templates for recurring problems in object-oriented software design. A pattern identifies the participating classes and objects, their roles, collaborations, and responsibility distribution, but it is not finished code—it must be adapted to a concrete context. The classic Gang of Four catalog defines 23 patterns grouped into creational patterns for object creation, structural patterns for composing classes and objects, and behavioral patterns for managing interaction and responsibility distribution.

## Why interviewers ask this

In low-level design interviews, design patterns usually surface inside a concrete task such as designing a parking lot, an undo feature, or a notification system. The interviewer is testing whether you can recognize a recurring design force, choose an appropriate abstraction, and explain the resulting coupling, extensibility, and complexity trade-offs. A pattern name without a justification for the variation it isolates is a weak answer.

## The core idea

Design patterns isolate the parts of a system that change. Creational patterns isolate object construction so code depends on interfaces or factories rather than concrete classes; structural patterns wrap or compose objects to control their interfaces and relationships; behavioral patterns separate communication and algorithms from the objects that trigger them. The value is not memorizing UML, but recognizing the forces—object creation, interface mismatch, one-to-many notification, algorithm variation—and applying a proven collaboration. Each pattern trades indirection or extra types for flexibility, and a strong candidate states that cost explicitly. In a low-level design interview, a good answer must say which class owns the abstraction, which object supplies the varying behavior, and what prevents change from rippling through the system.

## Key points

- The Gang of Four catalog organizes 23 patterns into creational, structural, and behavioral categories; creational patterns abstract object creation, structural patterns compose classes or objects, and behavioral patterns manage algorithm and responsibility distribution.
- Strategy encapsulates a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface; Java's Comparator passed to Collections.sort() varies sort order without changing the sort routine.
- Observer defines a one-to-many dependency between a subject and its observers, and it is the basis for many event-handling and publish-subscribe systems.
- Decorator wraps an object to add behavior without changing its interface; Java's BufferedInputStream adds buffering to any InputStream.
- Design patterns add classes and indirection, so a pattern should be applied only when there is a concrete axis of change that justifies the cost.

## Your 60-second answer

Design patterns are reusable solutions to recurring object-oriented design problems. They are not code you paste in; they are templates that describe roles, responsibilities, and collaborations. The classic catalog divides them into three groups: creational patterns like Factory Method and Singleton control object creation, structural patterns like Adapter and Decorator compose classes and objects, and behavioral patterns like Observer and Strategy manage communication and algorithms. I use them as shared vocabulary and to avoid reinventing fragile solutions. The main trade-off is overuse: applying a pattern where a simple function or class would do adds indirection and boilerplate. So in an interview I name the pattern, explain exactly what variation it isolates, and state what the extra classes cost in complexity.

## If they dig deeper

**What are the three categories of design patterns, and what problem does each category solve?**

Creational patterns abstract object creation so client code depends on interfaces or factories instead of concrete classes; examples include Singleton and Factory Method. Structural patterns compose classes or objects into larger structures, such as Adapter and Decorator. Behavioral patterns manage communication and the distribution of responsibilities among objects, such as Observer and Strategy.

**How is the Strategy pattern different from solving the same problem with inheritance?**

Strategy uses composition: a context holds a reference to a strategy interface, and the behavior can be swapped at runtime or supplied by the caller. Inheritance fixes the behavior at compile time and often leads to duplicated or overridden methods across subclasses. The cost of Strategy is extra objects and indirection.

**When would you choose Factory Method over Abstract Factory?**

Factory Method is appropriate when a creator class needs to defer instantiation to subclasses or when a single object's creation must vary. Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related products without naming concrete classes, so it is used when the system must be independent of how its products are created and must enforce that products from the same family are used together.

**How do design patterns differ from algorithms?**

An algorithm is a specific sequence of steps that solves a computational problem and has defined complexity. A design pattern is a higher-level template describing roles and relationships that must be adapted to a particular design; different implementations of the same pattern may use completely different algorithms and data structures.

**Why might Singleton be considered an anti-pattern in many systems?**

Singleton enforces a single instance and global access, which introduces hidden coupling, makes unit testing with mocks or parallel tests harder, and can hide lifecycle and dependency concerns. In dependency-injected systems, a container can manage a single instance without hard-coded global state. Singleton is still defensible when a resource such as a driver or configuration must be truly unique, but many uses are essentially global variables in disguise.

## Worked example

Consider sorting a list of Employee objects by salary, then by name, without rewriting the sort logic. In Java, Collections.sort(list, comparator) accepts a Comparator interface. One comparator that extracts getSalary() and compares integers implements the salary-order strategy; a second comparator that compares getName() implements the name-order strategy. The sort routine knows nothing about Employee fields—it only calls comparator.compare(a, b) and swaps based on the sign. Adding a third sort order means writing a new Comparator, not modifying the sort algorithm or the Employee class. The cost is one extra object per sort order and an extra method call on each comparison.

## Common traps

- Memorizing pattern names and UML diagrams without being able to explain which class owns the abstraction and what variation the pattern isolates.
- Applying a pattern because a question mentions design, when a simple class or standard library structure would be clearer.
- Confusing creational patterns with each other—for example, calling every factory method an Abstract Factory and missing the product-family distinction.
- Reciting a pattern's benefits while ignoring its costs, such as extra classes, indirection, or hidden global state in Singleton.

</details>

### 78. JWT · Medium

*system_design · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## sd-jwt` then `match: A developer writes the following JWT verification code. Whic`</sub>

**Question**

A developer writes the following JWT verification code. Which line is unsafe?

1. const token = req.headers.authorization.split(' ')[1];
2. const [headerB64, payloadB64, signatureB64] = token.split('.');
3. const header = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(headerB64, 'base64url').toString());
4. const payload = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(payloadB64, 'base64url').toString());
5. const signature = Buffer.from(signatureB64, 'base64url');
6. const key = header.alg === 'RS256' ? publicKey : secret;
7. const verified = crypto.verify(header.alg, Buffer.from(`${headerB64}.${payloadB64}`), key, signature);
8. if (!verified) throw new Error('Invalid signature');
9. if (payload.exp && Date.now() >= payload.exp * 1000) throw new Error('Token expired');
10. req.user = payload;

**Options**

A. const token = req.headers.authorization.split(' ')[1];
B. const [headerB64, payloadB64, signatureB64] = token.split('.');
C. const header = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(headerB64, 'base64url').toString());
D. const payload = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(payloadB64, 'base64url').toString());
E. const signature = Buffer.from(signatureB64, 'base64url');
F. const key = header.alg === 'RS256' ? publicKey : secret;
G. const verified = crypto.verify(header.alg, Buffer.from(`${headerB64}.${payloadB64}`), key, signature);
H. if (!verified) throw new Error('Invalid signature');
I. if (payload.exp && Date.now() >= payload.exp * 1000) throw new Error('Token expired');
J. req.user = payload;

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: F. const key = header.alg === 'RS256' ? publicKey : secret;

**Reference answer**

Line 6 is unsafe because it trusts the `alg` header to choose the verification key. An attacker can change `alg` to `HS256` and sign the token with the public key (which is often publicly known), causing the server to verify with the HMAC secret and accept a forged token. The algorithm must come from an allowlist, not from the token itself.

**Graded on**

- Never trust the `alg` header to select the verification key or algorithm.
- Use an allowlist of permitted algorithms and reject `alg: none`.
- Algorithm confusion attacks exploit servers that accept both HMAC and asymmetric signatures.
- The signature must be verified with the key and algorithm the server expects, not the token's claim.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

A JSON Web Token (JWT) is an open standard (RFC 7519) format for representing claims between parties as a compact, URL-safe string. It has three base64url-encoded parts: header, payload, and signature. The signature is computed over the header and payload with either a shared secret (HMAC) or a private key (RSA/ECDSA/EdDSA), allowing a server to verify integrity and authenticity without a session store. JWTs are commonly used as access tokens or ID tokens in OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect flows.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers at Google, Visa, and Gusto have used login-system design questions to see whether you can choose between stateful sessions and stateless tokens and defend the trade-offs. For JWT specifically, they are testing that you understand signing and verification, claim handling, expiration, token-theft risk, and why statelessness helps horizontal scaling.

## The core idea

A JWT is not encrypted by default; it is base64url-encoded and signed, so anyone who sees the token can read the payload. The signature allows the server to confirm the token was issued by a trusted party and was not tampered with, provided the verification key and algorithm are correct. Statelessness means each service can verify the token independently after checking its signature and expiry, with no shared session store. The cost is revoking a specific token before expiry requires extra state, such as a deny-list, short lifetimes with refresh tokens, or a token version checked against the user record.

## Key points

- A JWT is `base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature)` and the signature covers both header and payload.
- The payload is readable by anyone with the token, so never put secrets or plaintext passwords in a JWT.
- Use an allowlist of signing algorithms on verification, such as HS256 or RS256, and reject `alg: none`.
- For browser clients, prefer storing JWTs in httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies over localStorage to reduce XSS token theft; cookies then require CSRF protection.
- Stateless JWT verification scales horizontally, but revocation before expiry requires short lifetimes, refresh tokens, or a server-side denylist/version check.

## Your 60-second answer

A JWT is a compact, signed token that carries authentication and authorization claims without requiring server-side session state. It has three base64url-encoded parts: header, payload, and signature. The header declares the signing algorithm; the payload holds claims like sub, exp, and roles or scopes; the signature is computed over the first two parts. On login, the server verifies credentials and issues a signed JWT. On subsequent requests, the client sends it, usually in an Authorization header or a cookie, and the server verifies the signature and expiration and then trusts the claims. The main benefit is horizontal scaling: any service with the verification key can authenticate requests without hitting a shared session store. The trade-off is revocation: because the token is stateless, you usually handle logout by short expiration, refresh tokens, or checking a denylist.

## If they dig deeper

**How is a JWT different from a traditional session cookie?**

A session cookie stores only a random session ID in the client, while the server keeps the session data and must look it up on each request. A JWT carries the user identity and claims inside the token, so any server with the verification key can authenticate it without a shared session store. That removes a central lookup but makes immediate server-side revocation harder.

**What exactly happens when a server verifies a JWT?**

It splits the token into three parts, re-computes the signature over the encoded header and payload using the selected algorithm and key, and compares it to the provided signature. It must also confirm the algorithm is one it expects, not `none`, and check claims such as `exp`, `nbf`, `iss`, and `aud` before accepting the token.

**Where should a browser store a JWT?**

In most server-rendered browser apps, store it in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so JavaScript cannot read it and exfiltrate it through XSS. A cookie then needs CSRF protection. Storing in localStorage is easier for SPAs and API calls, but any XSS on the page can steal it directly.

**How do you revoke or log out a JWT before it expires?**

Keep access-token lifetimes short, minutes not days, and use a refresh token to obtain new access tokens. For immediate revocation, maintain a server-side denylist of `jti` values or a user/token version, and check it on each request. This reintroduces some server-side state.

**If an attacker steals a JWT, what stops them from reusing it until expiry?**

Nothing inherent in the token stops replay; expiry only bounds the window. You reduce risk with short expiry, refresh-token rotation, binding the token to the client via TLS or a fingerprint, and revoking compromised tokens through denylist or user-version checks, but a matching bearer token will be accepted until one of those controls fires.

## Worked example

Suppose a user logs in with email and password. The server verifies the password, then builds a header such as `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}` and a payload such as `{"sub":"user-123","exp":1710000000,"role":"admin"}`. It base64url-encodes both parts and computes an HMAC-SHA256 signature over `encodedHeader.encodedPayload` with a 256-bit secret. The token is the two encoded parts plus the signature, separated by dots. On the next request, the API takes the same encoded header and payload, recomputes HMAC-SHA256 with the same secret, and compares it in constant time to the third part. If it matches and the current time is before `exp`, the API trusts `sub` and `role` directly; no database or session lookup was needed.

## Common traps

- Calling JWTs encrypted: a standard JWT is signed and base64url-encoded, not encrypted, so a bearer can read its payload.
- Putting secrets like passwords, API keys, or internal user objects in the JWT payload.
- Trusting the `alg` header instead of using an algorithm allowlist, which enables `alg: none` and algorithm-confusion forgery attacks.
- Recommending localStorage for JWT storage without weighing XSS risk, or cookies without accounting for CSRF.

</details>

### 79. Aggregate functions · Medium

*sql · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## sql-aggregate-functions` then `match: Assemble the SQL clause that filters groups after aggregation, keeping only groups where t`</sub>

**Question**

Assemble the SQL clause that filters groups after aggregation, keeping only groups where the count of non-null values in the column 'employee_id' is greater than 5.

**Options**

**Tokens**: COUNT(employee_id), >, 5, HAVING

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- before: 3 → 0 · 0 → 1 · 1 → 2

**Reference answer**

HAVING COUNT(employee_id) > 5

**Graded on**

- HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
- COUNT(employee_id) counts non-null values in employee_id.
- The condition is > 5.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

SQL aggregate functions take a set of input rows and return a single scalar value for that set. The standard five are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX. With GROUP BY, the engine computes one result per group; without it, all rows passing WHERE form one group. Common implementations ignore NULLs except COUNT(*); engines add their own functions, such as SQL Server's STDEV/VAR and STRING_AGG (2017+).

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use aggregate-function questions to see whether you can actually write grouped reports and reason about how SQL evaluates them: which rows enter each group, what happens to NULLs, when to use HAVING, and when to use DISTINCT. They also test whether you know engine extensions and the difference between collapsing rows with aggregates and retaining rows with window functions.

## The core idea

Aggregation is about reducing row sets to one value per group, not just about the function names. GROUP BY defines the groups; without it, the whole result is a single group. Aggregates run after WHERE but before HAVING and ORDER BY in the logical query pipeline, so HAVING sees final group totals. COUNT(*) is the one standard core aggregate that counts rows containing NULLs; every other aggregate ignores NULL inputs. MIN/MAX measure extremes of any ordered type, while SUM/AVG accumulate scale-bearing values. Use aggregation when you need a summary; use window functions when you need row-level detail plus a summary.

## Key points

- COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values, and COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-NULL values.
- Every aggregate except COUNT(*) ignores NULL inputs; SUM and AVG of an empty set return NULL, while COUNT returns 0.
- MIN and MAX work on comparable types such as numbers, strings, and dates; in standard SQL and in PostgreSQL/Oracle, SUM and AVG also support interval/duration types, so they are not exclusively numeric.
- With GROUP BY, each group gets one aggregate result; HAVING filters after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters individual rows first.
- SQL Server 2017 added STRING_AGG for ordered string concatenation; PostgreSQL offers string_agg, array_agg, and percentile_cont as additional aggregates.

## Your 60-second answer

SQL aggregate functions reduce a group of rows to one scalar result. The core five are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-null values. All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs. MIN and MAX work on any comparable type: numbers, strings, and dates. SUM and AVG are defined for numeric types, and in standard SQL and engines such as PostgreSQL and Oracle they also accept interval types. With GROUP BY, each group gets one result; without GROUP BY, the whole table is one group. HAVING filters after aggregation, while WHERE filters rows before. Over an empty set, COUNT returns 0, but SUM and AVG return NULL. The main trade-off is that aggregate queries lose individual rows, so you must include any detail you still need through grouping or window functions.

## If they dig deeper

**How do the core aggregate functions treat NULL values?**

COUNT(*) counts all rows in the group, including rows with NULLs. Every other aggregate ignores NULL inputs: COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values, and SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX discard NULLs before computing. A column that is all NULL gives COUNT(column)=0 and MIN/MAX/SUM/AVG=NULL.

**Which aggregate functions can be used on dates, strings, or interval values?**

MIN and MAX work on any comparable type: numbers, strings according to collation, and dates/timestamps. SUM and AVG are defined for numeric types, and in standard SQL plus PostgreSQL and Oracle they also support interval/duration types. They do not operate on strings or booleans.

**What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING when working with aggregates?**

WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation, so it cannot reference aggregate results. HAVING runs after GROUP BY aggregation and can filter on COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. A query can use both: WHERE chooses source rows, HAVING chooses groups.

**What do SUM and AVG return when there are no matching rows?**

They return NULL, because there are no non-NULL values to combine. COUNT returns 0 for the same empty group. If you need 0 for SUM over no rows, wrap it in COALESCE.

**Why can joining tables make SUM and AVG return inflated values, and how do you avoid it?**

If one side has multiple rows per key in the other, the join fans out the fact rows and sums duplicates. Aggregate the finer-grained table first in a subquery or CTE, then join to the dimension table, so sums and averages operate on one row per fact.

## Worked example

Take a shifts table with rows: ('Ada', 30), ('Ada', NULL), ('Bea', 45), ('Cid', NULL). A grouped query selecting employee, COUNT(*), COUNT(minutes), SUM(minutes), AVG(minutes), MIN(minutes), and MAX(minutes) returns one row per employee with HAVING COUNT(minutes) > 0. Ada's COUNT(*) is 2 but COUNT(minutes) is 1 because one minute value is NULL; her SUM and AVG are both 30. Bea gets 1 row, 1 recorded minute, and SUM=AVG=45. Cid is removed by HAVING because no non-NULL minute values exist. In PostgreSQL, the same pattern works with an interval column: two intervals '00:30:00' and '00:45:00' sum to '01:15:00'.

## Common traps

- Using COUNT(column) when they meant row count, so NULL rows are silently excluded.
- Trying to filter aggregate values in WHERE; this fails because WHERE runs before aggregation.
- Expecting SUM/AVG over no rows to return 0; standard SQL returns NULL.
- Treating SUM/AVG as string or boolean functions; they are only defined for numeric and, in standard SQL/PostgreSQL/Oracle, interval inputs.

</details>

### 80. Heap / Priority Queue · Medium

*dsa · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## heap-priority-queue` then `match: Assemble the line that initializes a min-heap of size k for `</sub>

**Question**

Assemble the line that initializes a min-heap of size k for finding the kth largest element in a stream, using Python's heapq. The line should create an empty list and heapify it.

**Options**

**Tokens**: heapq.heapify, heap, =, [], (, )
**Fixed slots**: ·, ·, ·, ·, ·, ·

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- before: 0 → 4 · 4 → 1 · 1 → 5 · 2 → 3 · 3 → 0

**Reference answer**

The correct line is `heapq.heapify(heap)` after initializing `heap = []`. In Python, heapq operates on a list, and heapify converts the list into a valid min-heap in O(n) time. For an empty list, heapify is a no-op but establishes the heap invariant for subsequent pushes.

**Graded on**

- Python's heapq provides min-heap functions on a list.
- heapify transforms a list into a heap in O(n) time.
- For top-k largest, use a min-heap of size k.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

A binary heap is a complete binary tree, usually stored in an array, where every parent is <= its children in a min-heap or >= its children in a max-heap. The root is always the minimum or maximum element, readable in O(1); inserting an element or removing the root restores the heap property in O(log n). A priority queue is the abstract data type that returns elements by priority rather than arrival order, and heaps are its standard implementation. Default ordering differs by language: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap, C++ std::priority_queue is a max-heap, and Python's heapq provides min-heap functions on a list.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use heap problems to test whether you recognize repeated min/max queries over a changing collection and avoid sorting every time. Top-k, two-heap median, and k-way merge questions appear at companies like Meta, Apple, Spotify, Roblox, and Citadel. Strong answers show the correct heap orientation, when to bound heap size, and the difference between O(n) heap construction and O(log n) updates.

## The core idea

When a collection changes and the next operation is 'give me the smallest or largest so far', a heap keeps that extremum at the root with O(1) access and O(log n) updates. For top-k, keep a heap of size k: to find the kth largest, use a min-heap of the k largest candidates and discard anything smaller than the root. For median tracking, split the data into a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalancing after each insert. For merging multiple sorted streams, place the current head of each stream in a min-heap, pop the smallest, then push that stream's next element. The central choice is usually which heap orientation and size constraint make the desired rank directly accessible.

## Key points

- A binary heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property; in a 0-indexed array, the children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
- Insert and delete-min/max are O(log n); building a heap from n arbitrary elements by heapify is O(n), and reading the root is O(1).
- A priority queue is an abstract data type that removes elements by priority, not arrival order, and a heap is its standard implementation.
- For top-k, maintain a heap of size k: use a min-heap of the k largest for kth largest, and a max-heap of the k smallest for kth smallest.
- In Java, PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; in C++, std::priority_queue is a max-heap by default; Python's heapq implements a min-heap on lists.

## Your 60-second answer

A heap is a complete binary tree where every parent is <= or >= its children, so the root is the minimum or maximum. That gives O(1) access to the extremum and O(log n) insertion and deletion. A priority queue is the abstract interface that returns elements by priority, and a heap is the standard implementation. I reach for it when a collection keeps changing and I need the largest or smallest item repeatedly—top-k, scheduling, merging sorted streams, or tracking a median. For the kth largest I keep a min-heap of size k: each incoming element is compared with the root; if larger, I replace the root. The root is then the kth largest because it is the smallest of the k largest kept. For median, I split into a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half and rebalance after each insert. The tradeoff is that a heap only exposes the extremum efficiently, not arbitrary order or search.

## If they dig deeper

**How is a priority queue different from a normal FIFO queue?**

A FIFO queue removes elements in the order they arrived, regardless of their values. A priority queue removes the element with the highest or lowest priority first, so arrival order is not the deciding factor. Heaps implement priority queues because they can expose and update the extremum in logarithmic time.

**Why maintain only k elements in top-k instead of sorting the whole array?**

Sorting costs O(n log n) time and typically O(n) or O(log n) auxiliary space. A size-k heap costs O(n log k) time and O(k) space, which is better when k is much smaller than n. It also adapts naturally to a stream: each new element requires only O(log k) work to update the answer.

**Walk through the two-heap median structure.**

Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. After each insertion, rebalance so heap sizes differ by at most one, and ensure every lower half element is <= every upper half element. If total size is odd, the median is the top of the larger heap; if even, it is the average of the two heap tops.

**For Find Median from Data Stream, if all numbers are guaranteed to fall in [0,100], how would you optimize?**

Maintain an array of 101 counts and a running total. Each add increments one count in O(1). To find the median, walk the counts until reaching ceil(total/2), and for an even total continue to the next non-zero bucket to compute the average.

**If 99% of the numbers are in [0,100] but the rest can be anywhere, how would you optimize median tracking?**

Keep a 101-slot histogram for the [0,100] range and a separate rank-capable structure for outliers below 0 and above 100. Track total counts per region. To find the median, locate the middle index by skipping the below-zero region, then the histogram, then the above-100 region, which keeps the common case fast while still handling rare extreme values.

## Worked example

Find the 2nd largest in nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4]. Keep a min-heap of size 2. Process 3: heap is [3]. Process 2: heap is [2,3], root is 2. Process 1: root 2 is larger than 1, so discard 1. Process 5: root 2 is smaller than 5, so pop 2 and push 5; heap is [3,5]. Process 6: root 3 is smaller than 6, so pop 3 and push 6; heap is [5,6]. Process 4: root 5 is larger than 4, so discard 4. The root, 5, is the 2nd largest. The heap contains the two largest elements seen so far, and the root is the smaller of those two, which is exactly the kth largest.

## Common traps

- Using a max-heap of size k for kth largest and reporting its root: the root is the largest element, not the kth largest.
- Forgetting that building a heap from n arbitrary elements is O(n), not O(n log n); heapify is linear.
- Mixing up language defaults: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap, while C++ std::priority_queue is a max-heap by default.
- Returning the median in a two-heap structure without first rebalancing; one heap can drift and its top no longer represents the middle.

</details>

### 81. Polymorphism · Medium

*lld · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## lld-polymorphism` then `match: Assemble the definition of dynamic polymorphism by arranging`</sub>

**Question**

Assemble the definition of dynamic polymorphism by arranging the tokens in the correct order.

**Options**

**Tokens**: the receiver's runtime type, through a base or interface reference, and invoking them, in subclasses or implementations, with dispatch based on, Dynamic polymorphism is achieved by overriding methods

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- before: 5 → 3 · 3 → 2 · 2 → 1 · 1 → 4 · 4 → 0

**Reference answer**

Dynamic polymorphism is achieved by overriding methods in subclasses or implementations and invoking them through a base or interface reference, with dispatch based on the receiver's runtime type.

**Graded on**

- Dynamic dispatch selects the method implementation based on the actual object's type, not the variable's declared type.
- Overriding requires a method with the same signature in a subclass or implementation.
- The call is made through a reference of the supertype (base class, abstract class, or interface).

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Polymorphism lets a reference of a supertype (base class, abstract class, or interface) hold objects of different subtypes, and a method call on that reference runs the subtype's own override. The selection mechanism is runtime dynamic dispatch: the method implementation is chosen from the actual object's type, not the variable's declared type. Compile-time polymorphism, or overloading, is a separate mechanism where the compiler selects among same-named methods by static parameter types. In low-level design, dynamic polymorphism is the form that removes type conditionals and enables extension.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use this to test whether you can design around abstractions rather than concrete classes. They check for understanding of virtual dispatch, interface contracts, and the difference between overloading and overriding. A strong answer shows when polymorphism removes if/else and type checks, and when it does not.

## The core idea

The core is programming against a contract: a caller declares what it needs, such as an interface method, and not which class supplies it. Each concrete class implements the contract differently. At run time, the receiver's actual type selects the implementation. This keeps client code closed for modification when new types are added. The contract only works if subclasses honor the supertype's expected behavior; otherwise you reintroduce type checks. The cost is indirection and loss of local reasoning, because each call may run any implementation that honors the contract.

## Key points

- Dynamic polymorphism is achieved by overriding methods in subclasses or implementations and invoking them through a base or interface reference, with dispatch based on the receiver's runtime type.
- Compile-time polymorphism, or method overloading, chooses a method at compile time by static parameter types and is not based on the object's dynamic type.
- In Java, non-static, non-private instance methods are virtual by default; in C#, only methods marked virtual can be overridden through a base reference.
- Depend on abstractions, not concretions: passing interfaces or abstract classes lets new subclasses be added without changing client code.
- Replacing instanceof or switch-on-type chains with polymorphic method calls is the usual low-level design refactor, but only when the varying logic legitimately belongs to the type.

## Your 60-second answer

Polymorphism is using different concrete types through one interface, with each type providing its own behavior. You define an interface or abstract class that declares a method, then implement that method in multiple classes. When a caller invokes the method through a reference of the interface type, the runtime dispatches to the override on the actual object, not the reference. For example, checkout code can depend on PaymentMethod, and StripeProcessor or PayPalProcessor can be plugged in without changing checkout. This lets you add a new processor without editing existing client code, which is the main reason to use it in low-level design. The trade-off is indirection: the call site no longer shows exactly which code will run.

## If they dig deeper

**What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?**

Overloading gives multiple methods the same name but different parameter lists; the compiler picks one at compile time using the static types of arguments. Overriding keeps the same signature in a subclass and provides new behavior, with the runtime selecting the implementation based on the actual object type.

**When does Java use dynamic dispatch for a method call?**

For non-static, non-private instance methods, the JVM dispatches based on the receiver's runtime type. If the class overrides the method, that override runs; otherwise it walks up the superclass chain. Methods declared final cannot be overridden, so their implementation is fixed and the JIT can optimize them as non-virtual.

**How does polymorphism relate to the Liskov Substitution Principle?**

LSP requires a subclass to be substitutable for its superclass without causing incorrect behavior. Polymorphism depends on clients calling the supertype contract; if a subclass violates LSP by changing expected behavior or throwing unexpected exceptions, client code breaks and developers add instanceof checks to special-case it.

**In C#, what happens if I hide a base method with new instead of overriding it?**

The new keyword declares a new method that is not connected to the base method for polymorphism. If you call through a base reference, the base implementation runs; if through a derived reference, the derived implementation runs. To get runtime dispatch, the base method must be virtual and the derived method must use override.

**If behavior varies by combinations of two type hierarchies, how do you avoid instanceof chains?**

Use the visitor pattern or double dispatch. Each element class implements accept(visitor) and calls visitor.visit(this), so the concrete element type is passed to the visitor during dispatch. The visitor's overloaded visit methods then handle each element type, so variant behavior is selected by two runtime types without casts or instanceof.

## Worked example

Consider an interface PaymentMethod with method pay(int amount), and classes CreditCard and Wallet implementing it. Checkout stores a PaymentMethod and calls pay(total), so it only knows the abstraction. At runtime with a CreditCard, the JVM looks up pay in the CreditCard class and executes that version; with a Wallet, it executes Wallet's version. Adding a BankTransfer requires nothing more than a class implementing pay; Checkout does not change. If instead the system had a chain such as if (method instanceof CreditCard) else if (method instanceof Wallet), adding BankTransfer would require editing that chain. The polymorphic version moves the branch into the object's own type, implementing the Open/Closed principle.

## Common traps

- Claiming overloading is runtime polymorphism: overload resolution uses compile-time parameter types, so a reference typed as a superclass can select an unexpected overload.
- Believing Java instance methods are not virtual by default or C# methods are virtual by default; in Java, non-static, non-private instance methods are virtual, while C# requires virtual for overriding.
- Replacing every switch or if/else by polymorphism without considering whether the variation belongs to the type; logic that changes independently of the type may belong elsewhere.
- Using instanceof checks in a base class or client to produce type-specific behavior instead of putting that behavior in the class itself; this defeats the extension benefits.

</details>
